title: Dynamic 2D matrix transpose
instructorPromptText: Write a C program that dynamically allocates a 2D matrix of size R x C using pointer-to-pointer syntax (`int **matrix`). Read the matrix elements from the user, compute and print its transpose, and cleanly free all dynamically allocated memory.

specGateDimensions.description: Does the program correctly perform two-tier allocation (allocating the array of pointers `int**` and then looping to allocate each row `int*`)?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Dynamic 2D array allocation using pointers-to-pointers is a critical test of dynamic memory layout understanding in C.

specGateDimensions.description: Does the program free each individual row before freeing the main row-pointer array to avoid memory leaks?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Freeing only the outer pointer leaks the memory of all rows. The student must cleanly deallocate in reverse order of allocation.

specGateDimensions.description: Are the dimensions correctly swapped for the transposed matrix (e.g. loops run up to C for rows and R for columns)?
specGateDimensions.rationale: A common logical bug is keeping the original dimensions when printing or computing the transpose, resulting in buffer overflows.

expectedDivergences.pattern: Student calls `free(matrix)` without freeing each row pointer first, causing memory leaks.
Student allocates rows using R instead of C (or vice versa) for the transpose, causing segmentation faults on access.
Student accesses `matrix[i][j]` when the indexes exceed boundaries due to dimension confusion.
Student allocates a single flat array of size R * C and computes 2D offsets manually (e.g., `arr[i * C + j]`), which is an alternative layout.
Student forgets to validate if any `malloc` call inside the loop returns NULL.
